newsitem.title: USA: Attorneys general firm on right to sue tobacco cos.
newsitem.headline: Attorneys general firm on right to sue tobacco cos.

text.p: State attorneys general attempting to reach a landmark settlement with the tobacco industry said Wednesday they were determined to preserve individuals' right to sue cigarette makers.

The attorneys general said they are trying to find a solution that would give tobacco companies some certainty about the amounts they would have to pay in damages without depriving plaintiffs of their right to sue.
"I can conceive of ways to do it," said Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal. "You can be creative if you work with financing tools."
However, the attorneys general are united in their stance that they will not agree to a settlement that would give the industry total protection from lawsuits.
"If they are insisting on taking away a person's rights, then the chances of settlement are significantly diminished," Blumenthal said.

The attorneys general have sued the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. Also taking part in the negotiations are members of the health community and plaintiffs lawyers representing smokers and their families.
"This is going to be a good day," Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore told Reuters before the day's session began.

The attorneys general met in separate groups Tuesday and appeared to have developed one or more proposals that they presented to the industry late Tuesday afternoon. Both sides met into the early evening.
Although none of the attorneys general would give details on the discussions, they said they decided to continue talks with the industry on Wednesday because they felt progress was being made.

"The day we don't make progress and the day they don't exercise good faith is the day I leave. I'm coming back," said Washington Attorney General Christine Gregoire after the talks with tobacco representatives ended on Tuesday.

Moore and Richard Scruggs, a Mississippi lawyer assisting in the litigation, said that Wednesday's Wall Street Journal report on a tough proposal made by the tobacco industry was "old news" and that the negotiators were "way beyond that."
The report said the industry's plan would set stiff barriers for smokers seeking compensation, capping claims at $250,000 and barring punitive damages.
